articles.author: Alok Ranjan Daftuar
articles.description:
Every multi-tenant MCP deployment starts with the same instinct: put a tenant_id in the JWT, scope every tool call to it, and call the isolation problem solved. It isn't. The gap between "scoped by claim" and "actually isolated" is exactly where these deployments fail in production — not in testing, where a single code path is exercised, but in production, where a new tool handler forgets the filter, a cache key drops the tenant dimension, or an agent legitimately holds a valid token but aggregates a result that happened to include data from a neighboring tenant.
This article is about what real isolation looks like across three architectural patterns, which layer each one enforces, and how to test the boundary rather than just build it.
Multi-tenant MCP deployments settle into three recogn…
articles.title: Multi-Tenant MCP: Isolation Patterns That Hold Up

articles.description:
A shorter, code-first version of a guide first published on Omni Genz.
SDKs are handy, but for one or two endpoints they're often more than you need. Brevo's (formerly Sendinblue) REST API is plain JSON over HTTPS, so Node 18+ can talk to it with the built-in fetch. No extra packages.
This post walks through four things: checking your key, sending a simple email, sending with a saved template, and handling errors and rate limits properly.
In Brevo, go to Settings > SMTP & API and create an API key (it starts with xkeysib-). Put it in an environment variable, never in the repo:
export BREVO_API_KEY="xkeysib-..."

Every request sends the key in an api-key header. The base URL is https://api.brevo.com/v3.
Quick sanity check from the terminal before writing any code:
curl -s https://api.brevo.…

articles.author: dolai
articles.description:
Most guess-the-song games hand you thirty seconds of audio and let recognition do the work. By the time the chorus arrives, almost anyone can name the track. That is a fine party trick, but it makes for a weak scoring system, because the interesting question — how little do you actually need to hear? — never gets asked.
I spent some time with a browser game built entirely around that question. Each run holds five songs, and every one of them starts at a tenth of a second. You press play, hear what amounts to a click of sound, and then choose: commit to a guess now, or spend more of the clip and watch the payout shrink.
The scoring is where the design gets interesting
A song is worth 10,000 points at the shortest clip length. Every extension of the excerpt lowers that value, and a wrong gue…
articles.title: A music quiz where every song starts at a tenth of a second

articles.author: faliye
articles.description:
A while back I benchmarked llama.cpp on a 96GB GPU setup and found its concurrency behavior underwhelming.
That isn't llama.cpp's fault. From the start it was built to solve the capacity problem — "this model won't fit in one machine's VRAM" — not the throughput problem of many users hitting the server at once. If you're running a 70B or even 104B model at home for personal research or solo testing, "it runs at all" is the top priority. Under concurrency, when 10 users send requests at the same time, the engine should combine those 10 into a single Batch to keep the GPU busy. But the moment you batch them, the tensor volume moving between host A and host B blows up by orders of magnitude — from a few MB to tens or even hundreds of MB.
vLLM's whole architecture exists to solve high concurre…
articles.title: vLLM on 4 GPUs / 64GB: A Multi-Model Benchmark — For a Home Multi-Host Setup, I'd Go with vLLM
